h1: Exporting craft beer from India and the shelf life it needs
title: Exporting craft beer from India | Craft Beer School
desc: What exporting craft beer from India involves: the shelf life the beer must survive, oxygen, pasteurisation, cold chain, testing and the export paperwork.
teaser: A beer that tastes great in your taproom has to survive weeks at sea and months on a foreign shelf. That is a different product.
standfirst: Indian craft brewers increasingly ask about exporting. Before the paperwork, there is a technical question: can your beer survive the journey and still taste right on arrival? Here is what export demands of the liquid and the business.
sections:
A container leaving an Indian port sits on the dock, crosses warm seas, waits at the destination port, clears customs and then goes into the importer's warehouse before it reaches a shop. Weeks to months can pass between filling and the first sale. A standard container on a hot dock can get very warm inside.

Then it sits on a shelf. Importers usually want a good share of the shelf life left when the beer arrives, so a beer with a three-month best-before is often not exportable at all.

Oxidation is the main enemy of packaged beer: wet cardboard and honey in pale beers, faded hop aroma in hoppy ones. Heat speeds it up. For export you need to know your dissolved oxygen and total package oxygen and keep them low through transfers, carbonation and filling.

Brewers commonly aim for total package oxygen well under 100 ppb for beers meant to last. Hop-forward styles need lower still. If you cannot measure oxygen in the package, measuring it is the first investment to make before any export talk. Our guide to beer shelf life covers the other factors.

Unfiltered, unpasteurised beer is lovely fresh and risky on a long warm journey. Any spoilage organism that survived has weeks of heat to grow. For export, most brewers either pasteurise, sterile filter or run very tight hygiene with proven stability testing.

Tunnel pasteurisation for beer is often run somewhere around 15 to 25 pasteurisation units, enough for stability without cooking the flavour. Flash pasteurisation before kegging is another route. Either way, validate it with lab tests rather than assuming.

Run forced ageing tests: store samples warm for weeks, then taste them against cold-stored controls and check haze, oxygen pickup and flavour. These tests are a guide rather than an exact prediction, but a beer that falls apart after a few warm weeks will not survive a sea voyage.

Many brewers also hold back samples from each export batch and taste them at intervals, so they know how the beer is ageing in the importer's market.

Some styles travel better than others. Stronger, darker, malt-led beers and clean lagers with low oxygen hold up. Delicate hazy IPAs rely on freshness and are the hardest to export. Cans protect from light and usually let in less oxygen than crown-capped bottles, which is one reason export-focused brewers often choose them.

Ask about refrigerated containers for hoppy beers. They cost more, but if the brand depends on hop aroma, a warm voyage can undo it.

On the Indian side you will need an Importer Exporter Code from the DGFT, state excise permission to remove beer for export (often under bond, so state duty is not charged on exported beer) and the right customs documentation. Check whether your product also needs registration with an export promotion body such as APEDA. State procedures vary and change, so work with an export agent and your excise adviser.

On the destination side, the importer usually handles registration and label approval, but you supply the label in the language and format that market requires, often with a local importer address, allergen information and an alcohol statement. Labels approved for one country rarely work for another.

Export pricing is different from your taproom price. State duty is usually not charged on beer exported under bond, but you carry other costs: export packaging and pallets, freight to the port, sea freight, insurance, testing, any refrigerated container premium and the importer's and distributor's margins at the other end. Payment terms can be long. Currency also moves between order and payment.

Build a cost sheet per litre delivered to the importer, then work forward to the shelf price in the destination market. If your beer ends up priced well above local craft beer of similar quality, the order may happen once and never again.

Export suits breweries with stable, well-measured beer, packaging capacity to spare and a committed importer. It does not suit a brewpub looking for a quick extra sale. Start with one market, one importer and one or two beers that test well. Read about distribution at home to compare the effort against selling more in your own state.

The business side of export, from costing to choosing partners, is where most breweries need a plan before they need a pallet.
faqs: How long a shelf life does export beer need?
Long enough to cover weeks or months in transit and still leave the importer a good share of shelf life on arrival. Beers with a short best-before are rarely exportable.
Do I have to pasteurise export beer?
Not always, but you need proven microbiological stability. Most exporters pasteurise or sterile filter and confirm it with lab testing.
Clean lagers, stronger and darker malt-led beers with low package oxygen. Fresh hazy IPAs are the hardest to export.
What registrations does an Indian exporter need?
Typically an Importer Exporter Code and state excise permission for export, plus customs documents. Requirements vary by state and change, so use an export agent and excise adviser.
